- If sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.67) and forecast is trending up, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is strongly negative (≤ -0.33) and forecast is trending down, reduce downward slope or add a floor to prevent excessive sell-off.  
- After a sharp price spike, model tends to overcorrect — reduce forecast magnitude by 5–10% in next 3–5 days to avoid overshoot.  
- When true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 70), model often fails to adjust — apply a downward bias correction if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive.  
- If sentiment and price history show divergence (e.g., sentiment bullish but price drops), model may be misaligned — adjust forecast to reflect sentiment lag or reversal.  
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates downward moves in volatile periods — apply a 3–5% upward bias if sentiment is weak or neutral.  
- If true outcome is significantly below forecast (e.g., >10% drop), check if sentiment was bullish — if so, reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 5 days.  
- If true outcome is significantly above forecast (e.g., >10% rise), check if sentiment was bearish — if so, reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 5 days.  
- Model tends to ignore sentiment shifts in early days — apply a 1–2 day lag correction if sentiment changes sharply.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed, model often overestimates volatility — reduce forecast variance by 10–20% for next 7 days.
